title: Where we use electricity: from the wall and from cells

summary.text: In a power cut, the fan, the lights and the fridge stop at once, but the torch and the wall clock keep going. The things that stop get mains electricity, which comes along wires from a power station to the socket in the wall. The things that keep going carry their own cells, small stores of electricity. Your child listens to the appliances at home and names the job electricity does in each. Then they test old cells that the family thought were dead. Many cells that cannot light a torch still make a clock tick.
summary.art: A flat at night in a power cut: a still ceiling fan and a dark TV on one side, and a girl holding a glowing torch under a ticking wall clock on the other.

intro.hook: The power goes off on a hot evening. What stops working? What keeps going?
intro.text: Most children name the fan, the lights and the TV. But the torch still shines, and the wall clock still ticks. Why do some things stop and others keep going? The things that stop get electricity from the wall. The things that keep going carry their own small store of electricity, called a cell. In this unit you find out where wall electricity comes from, and you test how long a cell lasts.
intro.art: A child at a dark window in a power cut, holding a torch, with the street lights outside also dark.

outcomes: By the end I can name things at home that use electricity to make light, sound, heat, cold and movement.
By the end I can say that mains electricity comes along wires from a power station to the sockets in the wall.
By the end I can tell which things use mains electricity and which use cells, and say what keeps working in a power cut.
By the end I can test old cells in a torch and a clock, and say what I found.
By the end I can explain why a cell that cannot light a torch may still run a clock.
By the end I can give the safety rules for mains electricity and for cells, with a reason for each.

terms.meaning: Electricity is a kind of energy that flows along wires and makes things work.
terms.example: Electricity flowing into a fan makes the fan's blades turn.
terms.art: A ceiling fan turning, with a thin glowing line running along its wire into the ceiling.

terms.meaning: An appliance is a machine at home that uses electricity to do a job.
terms.example: A fan, a fridge, a mixie, a TV and a torch are all appliances.
terms.art: A row of five small pictures: a fan, a fridge, a mixie, a TV and a torch.

terms.meaning: Mains electricity is the strong electricity that comes along wires from a power station to the sockets in the wall. It is strong enough to kill a person.
terms.example: The fridge, the TV and the geyser use mains electricity through a plug in the wall.
terms.art: A plug going into a wall socket, with a thick wire leading out of the building to a pole outside.

terms.meaning: A socket is the place in the wall where mains electricity comes out. A plug on the end of an appliance's wire fits into it.
terms.example: A grown-up pushes the mixie's plug into the socket in the kitchen.
terms.art: A white three-pin plug next to a wall socket with a switch beside it.

terms.meaning: A power station is a big building where mains electricity is made.
terms.example: The power station at the Idukki dam in Kerala makes electricity from falling water.
terms.art: A big dam in green hills, with water rushing out at the bottom beside a power station building.

terms.meaning: A cell is a small store of electricity that you can carry. Many people call it a battery.
terms.example: A torch, a TV remote and a wall clock run on cells.
terms.art: Three cells of different sizes lying side by side: a long AA cell, a thin AAA cell and a flat round button cell.

terms.meaning: A rechargeable battery is a store of electricity that can be filled again from the wall. Filling it is called charging.
terms.example: A phone has a rechargeable battery inside. We charge it from a socket.
terms.art: A phone lying on a table with its charger wire going to a wall socket and a battery sign on its screen.

terms.meaning: A power cut is a time when mains electricity stops coming to a home or a street.
terms.example: In a power cut, the fans stop, but a torch still works.
terms.art: A street at night with all the windows dark, except one where a torch is shining.

explanations.concept: Electricity does many jobs at home
explanations.definition: Electricity is a kind of energy. Appliances change it into light, sound, heat, cold or movement.
explanations.description: In the Listen to the Electricity activity, you heard the fan whirr and the fridge hum. When the switch went off, the sound stopped. Electricity was doing a job in each one. A bulb changes electricity into light. A doorbell changes it into sound. An iron and a geyser change it into heat. A fridge uses it to make cold. A fan and a mixie use it to make movement. Some appliances do two jobs at once. A TV makes light and sound.
examples: A tube light changes electricity into light.
A mixie changes electricity into movement, so the blade spins and grinds the chutney.
A fridge uses electricity to keep curd and milk cold.
explanations.art: A cut-away drawing of a flat with small signs by each appliance: a sun by the light, a music note by the TV, a flame by the iron, a snowflake by the fridge and a spinning arrow by the fan.

explanations.concept: Mains electricity comes from a power station along wires
explanations.definition: Mains electricity is made in power stations. It travels along wires, on poles or under the ground, to every building and then to the sockets in the walls.
explanations.description: Every appliance with a plug gets its electricity from the wall. The wall does not make it. Wires bring it from a power station, often very far away. First come big wires on tall towers, then wires on street poles, then a wire to your building's meter box and into your wall. Power stations make electricity from coal, falling water, wind, sunlight and other fuels. In India, most of it comes from burning coal. If a wire on the way is broken, everyone after it has a power cut.
examples: The Idukki dam in Kerala uses falling water to make electricity.
Near Kanyakumari in Tamil Nadu, hundreds of tall windmills make electricity from the wind.
At Pavagada in Karnataka, a huge field of solar panels makes electricity from sunlight.
explanations.art: A long picture from left to right: a power station, tall towers with wires, a pole on a city street, a building's meter box and a fan in a flat.

explanations.concept: A cell is a store of electricity that runs down slowly
explanations.definition: A cell holds chemicals that make electricity flow when the cell is in a torch, a clock or a toy. As the cell is used, the chemicals change, and the cell gives less and less.
explanations.description: A cell is a small store of electricity that you can carry. That is why a torch works in a power cut. Inside a cell are chemicals. When the cell is used, they slowly change and make electricity flow. A cell runs down little by little. In the Tired Cell Test, some cells could not light the torch but still made the clock tick. A torch needs a lot of electricity every second. A clock needs only a tiny amount. A phone's battery is a store you can fill again from the wall.
examples: In the Tired Cell Test, an old cell that could not light the torch often still ran the wall clock.
A wall clock can run for many months on one cell.
A phone battery runs down faster when the torch and the screen are both on.
explanations.art: Three drawings of the same AA cell, side by side, with a level line inside dropping lower each time, and a torch above the first and a clock above the last.

explanations.definition: Nerves in animals, including us, send messages as tiny electric signals. Plants also send electric signals through their bodies.
explanations.description: Your body has no plug and no cell, but it uses electricity all the time. Tiny electric signals run along your nerves when you touch something. A tiny electric signal also starts every beat of your heart. The energy for these signals comes from the food you eat. Plants send electric signals too. Touch a touch-me-not plant, and a signal runs along her stalk. Her leaves fold within seconds. Scientists still argue about whether the plant feels the touch.
examples: A doctor's ECG machine shows the electric signals of a beating heart as a wavy line.
A touch-me-not plant folds her leaves after a touch, and an electric signal runs along her stalk first.
Jagadish Chandra Bose, a scientist in Kolkata, measured electric signals in plants more than a hundred years ago.

perspectives.who: A plain fact, from the work of J. C. Bose and many plant scientists since
perspectives.explanation: A plant senses a touch, sends the news along her body as an electric signal, and acts on it. That is sensing and deciding, done without a brain.
These scientists say a plant's signal is an automatic response, like a reflex, and needs no feeling.

explanations.art: A touch-me-not plant with one leaf folding after a child's fingertip touches it, and a faint glowing line running down the stalk.

agreed.text: Mains electricity is made in power stations and reaches homes along wires.
agreed.evidence: When a wire on the street breaks or a power station stops, every home after it has a power cut until the fault is fixed.

agreed.text: A cell stores electricity using chemicals, and runs down as it is used.
agreed.evidence: A torch left on gets dimmer or stops, and a new cell makes it work again. Alessandro Volta made the first battery in Italy in 1800.

agreed.text: Mains electricity can kill a person, but the small cells in a torch are not strong enough to give a shock.
agreed.evidence: Indian homes get mains electricity at about 230 volts. An AA cell gives only 1.5 volts, which you cannot feel through dry skin.

challenging.claim: The electricity is made in the socket, or in the switch.
challenging.who: A common idea among young children
challenging.for: When you press the switch, the light comes on at once. It looks as if the switch makes it.
challenging.against: In a power cut, pressing the switch does nothing. The switch only opens and closes the path. The electricity comes along wires from a power station.
challenging.context: This card is about where the electricity in the wall comes from.

challenging.claim: A cell is either new or dead. A dead cell has nothing left.
challenging.for: A torch with old cells goes dark, so the cells seem empty.
challenging.against: In the Tired Cell Test, many old cells that could not light the torch still made the clock tick. They still held some electricity, but too little for the torch.
challenging.context: This card is about whether old cells are really empty.

challenging.claim: Cells are small and safe, so they are fine for little children to play with.
challenging.for: An AA cell is too weak to give you a shock.
challenging.against: A swallowed button cell can badly burn a small child's insides within two hours. Old cells can leak a chemical that hurts skin and eyes. Cells are safe to use, but not to play with.
challenging.context: This card is about staying safe with cells.

challenging.claim: Only animals with a brain use electric signals.
challenging.for: We know about nerves and brains, and they work with electric signals.
challenging.against: Plants send electric signals too. A touch-me-not folds her leaves after a signal runs along her stalk. Some scientists call this a reflex, not a feeling.
challenging.context: This card is about which living beings use electricity.

big_questions.q: In the Tired Cell Test, some cells could not light the torch but still ran the clock. Were those cells empty or not?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the cell could still do, and what it could not.

big_questions.q: Where does the electricity in your wall start? Can you follow it all the way back?
big_questions.hint: Think of the wires on the street, the power station, and what the power station uses: coal, falling water, wind or sunlight.

big_questions.q: Your heart beats with tiny electric signals, but you have no plug and no cell. Where does your electricity come from?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you eat, and where your food got its energy.

big_questions.q: People lived for thousands of years without electricity. What would you miss most? What would you not miss at all?
big_questions.hint: Ask a grandparent or an older neighbour what life was like before electricity came to their home.

story.title: The Night the Lift Stopped
story.note: Anju, Rahul, Ammamma, Amma and Thresiamma are made up. Ammamma means grandmother in Malayalam. Many homes in Kerala villages had no electricity in the 1960s, and grinding stones were used by hand before mixies.
text: Anju was seven. She lived on the sixth floor of a tall building in Kochi, in Kerala.

One hot evening in April, she was doing her homework under the ceiling fan. Her cousin Rahul, who was five, was watching cartoons. Ammamma, her grandmother, was grinding coconut in the mixie for chutney.
Then, all at once, everything stopped.
The fan slowed down and went still. The TV went black. The mixie gave one last whirr. The lights went out, and the flat was dark.
'Power cut!' shouted Rahul.
From the corridor came voices. 'The lift has stopped!' someone called. 'Is anyone inside?' It was Thresiamma aunty from next door. Luckily, the lift was empty.
Ammamma felt her way to the kitchen drawer and found the torch. She clicked it on. A round circle of light jumped onto the wall.
'Why does the torch still work?' asked Rahul. 'Everything else stopped.'

Anju thought about it. She shone the torch on the mixie. Its wire went to a plug in the wall. She shone it on the TV. Its wire went to the wall too. Then she looked at the torch in her hand. It had no wire at all.
'I think I know,' she said. 'The TV and the mixie get their electricity from the wall. When the wall stops, they stop.'
'And the torch?' asked Rahul.
Anju twisted open the back of the torch. Inside were two cells, like short, fat pencils with metal ends. 'The torch carries its own electricity,' she said. 'It keeps it in these cells.'
Tick, tock, went the clock on the wall. Rahul looked up. 'The clock didn't stop either!'
Ammamma lifted the clock down. On the back was one small cell.
Then Rahul heard music. Ammamma's old radio on the shelf was still playing film songs, very softly. It had cells too.
Amma's phone buzzed on the table. 'A phone has no cells,' said Rahul. 'But it still works.'
'A phone has a battery inside it,' said Ammamma. 'We fill it from the wall when we charge it. Then it carries the electricity with it, like a water bottle you fill at the tap.'
By torchlight, Anju made a list on the back of her homework. On one side she wrote STOPPED: fan, TV, mixie, lights, fridge, lift. On the other side she wrote KEPT GOING: torch, clock, radio, phone.
'Everything that stopped has a wire to the wall,' she said. 'Everything that kept going carries its own store.' Then she frowned. 'But where does the wall get its electricity?'
Ammamma took them out to the balcony. The whole street was dark. Not one window was lit.

'Look at those wires on the poles,' Ammamma said. 'They carry electricity to every building, from a power station far away. Tonight something is wrong on the way. So the whole street has a power cut.'
'Even the ice cream shop downstairs?' asked Rahul.
'Even the ice cream shop,' said Ammamma.
Rahul groaned. He was getting hot. Ammamma picked up a palm-leaf fan and waved it over him.

'When I was your age, in our village near Thrissur, there was no electricity at all,' she said. 'Every night we used a fan like this one. We had a kerosene lamp for light. My mother ground the rice for dosa on a big stone, by hand.'
'No TV?' asked Rahul.
'No TV,' said Ammamma, and she laughed.
Anju looked at her list again. 'Ammamma, your mixie needs the wall. But your mother's grinding stone needed only her arms.'
'And her arms ran on breakfast,' said Ammamma.
Just then, with a click, the fan began to turn. The lights flashed on. From every flat in the building came a cheer.
Anju drew a little plug at the top of her first list, and a little cell at the top of the second. Then she showed Rahul.
'Now you know what to do in a power cut,' she said. 'Look for the things that carry their own cells.'
story.epiphany: For the parent: in the power cut, Anju sorts the flat into things that stopped and things that kept going. Everything that stopped had a wire to the wall, which brings mains electricity from a power station. Everything that kept going carried its own cells, or a battery charged earlier from the wall.
ask: In the power cut, what stopped working in Anju's flat? What kept going?
How did Anju work out why the torch still worked?
Ammamma said a phone battery is like a water bottle. What did she mean?
Why did the whole street have a power cut, and not only Anju's flat?
art: A girl doing homework under a ceiling fan while her small cousin watches TV and her grandmother runs a mixie.
The same flat in darkness, with the grandmother holding up a torch whose circle of light falls on a still mixie.
The girl writing two lists by torchlight, headed 'STOPPED' and 'KEPT GOING', with a wall clock above her.
A grandmother and two children on a balcony looking down at a dark street with wires on poles.

experiments.title: The Tired Cell Test: can a cell that fails the torch still run a clock?
experiments.context: In this experiment you collect old cells that your family thinks are used up. You try each one in a torch and in a wall clock. A torch needs a lot of electricity. A clock needs very little.
experiments.question: Old cells cannot light a torch any more. Do they still hold any electricity? Can they still run a wall clock?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will an old cell that cannot light the torch make the clock tick? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same torch and the same clock for every cell. We watch the clock's second hand for the same time, 10 seconds, for every cell. We also try new cells in both, so we know the torch and the clock work.

materials.item: old AA cells from remotes, toys, clocks or the drawer, at least 4 and 6 if you can (ask neighbours if you have none)
one or two new AA cells, as many as your torch takes
a torch that takes AA cells
a wall clock or table clock that takes one AA cell
small paper stickers or masking tape, and a pen, to number the cells
paper and a pencil for the results table

experiments.safety: If a cell has a white or green crust, or feels wet, do not touch it with bare hands. Put it in a paper bag for e-waste, and wash your hands. Never open a cell or put it in your mouth. Keep button cells away from small children.

schedule.what: Number the old cells, guess, test each one in the torch and in the clock, and count the results.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with a tick or a cross for the torch and the clock. Then colour each cell's sticker: green if it ran both, yellow if it ran only the clock, red if it ran nothing.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results for 6 old cells

data.label: Lit the torch and ran the clock

setup.art: A small heap of old AA cells on a steel plate, each with a paper sticker numbered 1 to 6, beside a torch and a wall clock lying on the table.
setup.caption: 1. Collect old cells. Number each one.

setup.art: A girl putting cells into the back of a torch and shining it at a white wall, where no light shows.
setup.caption: 2. Try the old cells in the torch. Does it light?

setup.art: The same girl putting one cell into the back of a wall clock and watching its thin red second hand move.
setup.caption: 3. Try each cell in the clock. Watch the second hand for 10 seconds.

setup.art: A results table with ticks and crosses, and the cells sorted into three groups with green, yellow and red stickers.
setup.caption: 4. Sort the cells into three groups.

flow.do: 1. Collect the old cells together. 2. Stick a numbered sticker on each one. 3. Check each cell for crust or leaks.
flow.say: These cells were taken out because they stopped working. Let's give each one a number.
flow.kid: Help collect old cells. Stick a number on each.
flow.parent: Look at every cell before your child holds it. Put aside any cell with white or green crust, or a wet look, in a paper bag. Most homes find old cells in remotes, toys, a drawer or a stopped clock.

flow.do: 1. Put the new cell or cells in the torch, and one new cell in the clock, to show both work. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Write the guess.
flow.say: The new cell lights the torch and runs the clock. Now, will an old cell run the clock? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Will an old cell run the clock? Why do you think so?

good: Maybe, because the clock is small.
Some might, because they are not all the same age.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Write it down and do not say what will happen. If your torch takes two cells, you will test the old cells two at a time in it (1 and 2, then 3 and 4, then 5 and 6). Then you test each cell alone in the clock.

flow.do: 1. Put an old cell in the torch (two cells, if it takes two). 2. Point it at a wall and switch it on. 3. Mark a tick if it lights, a cross if not. 4. Do the same for the other cells. If you test two cells together, both get the same mark.
flow.say: Put cell number 1 in the torch. Switch it on. Does it light the wall? Tick or cross?
flow.kid: Put a cell in the torch. Switch it on. Does it light?
flow.parent: A dim glow counts as a tick, but say it was dim. If the torch is dim or dark with a pair, mark a cross for both cells. Many torches today have bright white lights, called LEDs, that go dark suddenly when cells are weak.

flow.do: 1. Put an old cell in the clock. 2. Count to ten while you watch the second hand. 3. Mark a tick if it moved, a cross if not. 4. Do the same for every cell.
flow.say: Now put cell number 1 in the clock. Watch the second hand while we count to ten. Did it move?
flow.kid: Put the cell in the clock. Watch the thin hand. Did it move?
flow.parent: Put the cell in the right way round. Match the little plus sign on the cell with the plus sign in the clock. A clock that runs, even slowly, counts as a tick.

flow.do: 1. Count the ticks in each column. 2. Sort the cells into three groups: ran both, ran only the clock, ran nothing. 3. Ask what your child found, and why. 4. Ask the check question.
flow.say: How many cells lit the torch? How many ran the clock? What did you find out? Why do you think that happened?
flow.kid: Count your ticks. Which worked with more cells, the torch or the clock? Why?

ask.q: Why did some cells run the clock but not the torch?
good: They had a little electricity left.
The torch needs a lot and the clock needs a little.

flow.parent: Wait for your child to say what they found and how they know. Then say it plainly: the old cells still held some electricity. The torch needs a lot every second, so it stopped. The clock needs very little, so it kept going. If every cell ran both, your cells were not so old. If none ran the clock, they were truly used up. Both are real results. Put the cells that ran only the clock in a clock or a remote. Take the cells that ran nothing to an e-waste box.

check.q: A cell cannot light the torch, but it makes the clock tick. What does that show?
options: The cell still has a little electricity
The clock makes its own electricity
check.why: The clock only ticks if electricity flows from the cell. So the cell still had some, but too little for the torch. 'Completely empty' is a common guess, but the clock shows it is not true.

experiments.title: The Phone Battery Race: which job uses up the battery faster?
experiments.context: In this experiment you watch a phone's battery number. First the phone rests with its screen off. Then it plays a video with its torch on. A phone battery is a store of electricity that is filled from the wall.
experiments.question: Does a phone's battery go down faster when the phone is resting, or when it plays a video with its torch on?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the battery number drop more in the 8 minutes of resting, or in the 8 minutes of video with the torch on? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same phone, not charging, for both tests. Each test lasts exactly 8 minutes on a timer. We read the battery number at the start and at the end of each test.

materials.item: a grown-up's phone with at least half its battery left, not on the charger
a timer, such as a kitchen timer or another phone
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Read the battery, let the phone rest for 8 minutes, then play a video with the torch on for 8 minutes, and compare the drops.

experiments.record: Write the battery number before and after each test. Draw a bar for how much it dropped in each test.

setup.art: A phone lying face down on a table beside a kitchen timer and a sheet of paper with a battery number written on it.
setup.caption: 1. Write the battery number. Let the phone rest for 8 minutes.

setup.art: The same phone standing up, playing a cartoon with its back torch shining on the ceiling, beside the timer.
setup.caption: 2. Now play a video with the torch on for 8 minutes. Write the number again.

flow.do: 1. Find the battery number on the phone. 2. Show it to your child. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: This number shows how full the phone's battery is. A hundred means full. Which will make it drop more: resting, or playing a video with the torch on? Why?
flow.kid: This number shows how full the battery is. Which will empty it faster: resting, or playing a video with the torch on?
flow.parent: Take the phone off the charger first. On many phones you see the number by pulling down from the top of the screen or in the battery settings.

flow.do: 1. Write the battery number. 2. Lock the phone and put it face down. 3. Set the timer for 8 minutes. 4. Write the number again.
flow.say: The phone is resting now. While we wait, let's draw what the phone is doing. After 8 minutes, read the number again.
flow.kid: Write the number. Let the phone rest. Read it again after 8 minutes.
flow.parent: Use the 8 minutes for the drawing, or play the Power Cut card game. The number may not move at all. That is a result too.

flow.do: 1. Write the number. 2. Play a cartoon at full brightness. 3. Switch on the phone's torch. 4. After 8 minutes, write the number again.
flow.say: Now the phone has two jobs: playing a video and shining its torch. Watch for 8 minutes, then read the number.
flow.kid: Now the video and the torch are on. Read the number after 8 minutes.
flow.parent: The drop is usually a few points, for example from 70 to 67. It depends on the phone. The resting test usually drops 0 or 1. If both drops are the same, run the video test for longer.

flow.do: Work out each drop together. Ask what your child found and why. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: How much did the number drop in each test? Which job used more electricity? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which test made the number drop more? Why?

ask.q: Why did the video and torch empty the battery faster?
good: The torch and the screen need lots of electricity.
The phone was doing more work.

check.q: A phone's battery drops 3 points in a video test and 0 points while resting. What does that show?
options: Making light and pictures uses more electricity than resting
The battery fills up when the phone rests
check.why: The battery is a store. The bright screen and the torch took electricity out of it faster. A resting phone uses only a little, but it does not fill up again without a charger.

activities.title: Listen to the Electricity: what goes quiet when a switch goes off?
activities.context: In this activity you sit very still with your eyes shut and listen to your home. A grown-up switches things off one at a time at their switches. You say what went quiet, and what job that thing was doing.

materials.item: a quiet room near the kitchen, with the fan and lights on
a sheet of paper with five boxes: Light, Sound, Heat, Cold, Movement
a pencil

activities.safety: Only the grown-up presses the switches. Children do not touch switches, plugs or sockets with wet hands.

schedule.what: Listen with eyes shut while a grown-up switches things off. Name each thing and its job, and draw it in a box.

activities.record: Draw each thing in the box for its job. A thing that does two jobs goes in two boxes.

setup.art: A boy sitting cross-legged on the floor with his eyes shut, while a ceiling fan turns above him and a fridge stands in the kitchen behind.
setup.caption: 1. Shut your eyes. Listen to your home.

setup.art: A mother pressing a switch on a switchboard while the boy points up at the fan slowing down, and a paper with five boxes lies beside him.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up switches one thing off. What went quiet? Draw it in a box.

flow.do: 1. Sit together with eyes shut for one minute. 2. Ask your child to count the sounds they hear.
flow.say: Shut your eyes. Listen to our home for one minute. How many sounds can you hear? Which ones come from electricity?
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Listen. How many sounds can you hear?
flow.parent: Good sounds to hear are the fan, the fridge hum, a tube light's buzz, the water purifier or a TV. Birds, traffic and people talking are not electricity.

flow.do: 1. Switch off one thing, such as the fan, the fridge or a light. 2. Your child opens their eyes and says what stopped. 3. Ask what job it was doing. 4. Switch it back on. Do this for four things.
flow.say: Something just went quiet. What was it? What job was electricity doing in it: light, sound, heat, cold or movement?
flow.kid: Something went quiet. What was it? What job did it do?
flow.parent: Switch the fridge off at its own wall switch for only a few seconds, then back on. Its hum may take a moment to stop. A light makes no sound, so ask your child to open their eyes for that one.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws each thing in its job box. 2. Count how many things are in each box. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Draw each thing in the box for its job. Which box has the most?
flow.kid: Draw each thing in its box. Which box has the most?

check.q: A fan uses electricity to do which job?
check.why: Electricity turns the fan's blades, so it makes movement. The moving air feels cool on your skin, but the fan does not make the air colder.

activities.title: Follow the Wire: from your fan back to the power station
activities.context: In this activity you follow the path of mains electricity backwards, from the fan in your room to the wires on the street. Then you draw the whole path, out to the power station.

materials.item: a window or balcony where you can see poles, wires or a building's meter box
a long strip of paper and crayons

activities.safety: Look only. Never touch a meter box, a pole, a fallen wire or a wire that sparks. Tell a grown-up at once if you see one.

schedule.what: Follow the fan's wire to the switchboard, find the meter, look at the street wires, and draw the path to the power station.

activities.record: Draw the path on a long strip of paper: the fan, the switch, the meter, the street pole, the tall towers and a power station at the end.

setup.art: A girl and her mother on a balcony, pointing at black wires running from a pole to their building.
setup.caption: 1. Find where the wires come to your building.

setup.art: A long strip of paper with a drawing from left to right: a fan, a switch, a meter, a pole, a tall tower and a power station.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the whole path, from the power station to your fan.

flow.do: 1. Stand under the fan. 2. Show the switch on the switchboard that turns it on. 3. Ask where the electricity comes into the switch from.
flow.say: When I press this switch, the fan turns. Where do you think the electricity comes from before the switch?
flow.kid: Where does the fan's electricity come from? Guess.

ask.q: Where does the electricity come from?

flow.parent: Many children say the switch or the wall makes it. Don't correct the guess yet. The walk will answer it.

flow.do: 1. Show the meter or the main switch box of your home, if you can. 2. Then look out of a window or balcony for poles and wires.
flow.say: This meter counts how much electricity our home uses. Now look outside. Can you see wires that bring electricity to our building?
flow.kid: Look at the meter. Now look outside. Can you see the wires?
flow.parent: In many flats the meters are in a room on the ground floor. Looking from the doorway is enough. In some cities the wires run under the ground, so you may see only a box on the pavement.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that the wires go back to a power station. 2. Name what power stations use: coal, falling water, wind or sunlight. 3. Your child draws the whole path.
flow.say: The wires go all the way back to a power station, often very far away. Some power stations burn coal. Some use falling water, wind or sunlight. Draw the path.
flow.kid: Draw the path from the power station to your fan.

check.why: Mains electricity is made in a power station and comes along wires. The switch only lets it through or stops it. In a power cut, the switch does nothing.

activities.title: Before the Wires: ask an older person about life without electricity
activities.context: In this activity you ask a grandparent or an older neighbour how people did their jobs before their home had electricity. You make a picture chart: then and now.

materials.item: a grandparent, an older relative or an older neighbour, in person or on a phone call
a sheet of paper folded in half, headed Then and Now
a pencil and crayons

schedule.what: Ask four questions about life before electricity, then draw a then-and-now chart.

activities.record: On the Then side, draw how a job was done without electricity. On the Now side, draw the appliance that does it today.

setup.art: A girl holding a phone on a video call with an old woman who is showing a palm-leaf fan.
setup.caption: 1. Ask an older person four questions.

setup.art: A folded paper with Then on one side, showing a kerosene lamp and a grinding stone, and Now on the other, showing a bulb and a mixie.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a then-and-now chart.

flow.do: Help your child choose four questions to ask. Suggest these: How did you get light at night? How did you keep cool? How did you grind food? How did you keep milk fresh?
flow.say: Before we call, let's choose four questions. What would you like to know about life without electricity?
flow.kid: Choose four questions to ask about life without electricity.
flow.parent: If no older person can talk today, ask a neighbour, or use the questions as a guessing game and check them later.

flow.do: Your child asks the questions. Help them listen and remember each answer.
flow.say: Ask your first question. Listen to the whole answer. What did they use instead?
flow.kid: Ask your questions. Listen well. What did they use?
flow.parent: Typical answers are oil lamps or kerosene lanterns, hand fans, a grinding stone, boiling milk twice a day, and a clay pot for cool water. Some older people got electricity only as adults.

flow.do: Your child draws the then-and-now chart and tells you one thing that surprised them.
flow.say: Draw each job: how it was done then, and how it is done now. What surprised you most?
flow.kid: Draw then and now. What surprised you most?

ask.q: Which old way did not need electricity at all?
good: The grinding stone. It needed only arms.
The clay pot kept water cool.

flow.think: Which of the old ways do people still use today?

games.title: Power Cut! a card game: what keeps working?
games.context: This is a card game for 2 to 4 players. You collect appliance cards for your home. When a Power Cut card comes up, every plug appliance stops and you lose it. Cell appliances keep working.

items.b: Plug: stops in a power cut
Plug: stops in a power cut
Plug: stops in a power cut
Plug: stops in a power cut
Plug: stops in a power cut
Plug: stops in a power cut
Plug: stops in a power cut
Plug: stops in a power cut
Plug: stops in a power cut
Plug: stops in a power cut
Plug: stops in a power cut
Plug: stops in a power cut

rules: Shuffle the 24 appliance cards and the 4 Power Cut cards together, with the appliance names face up and the backs hidden. Put them in one pile.
Take turns. On your turn, take the top card.
If it is an appliance, say 'plug' or 'cell' before you turn it over. Turn it over to check. If you were right, keep the card in front of you. If you were wrong, put it in the out pile.
If it is a Power Cut card, every player checks their cards. Every plug appliance stops working and goes to the out pile. Cell and charged battery cards stay.
When the pile is finished, count your cards. The player with the most cards still working wins.

setup.art: A pile of cards on a floor mat, with a fan and a torch drawn on the two top cards, and two children sitting beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle all the cards into one pile.

setup.art: A child turning over a card that says 'POWER CUT!' while another child sadly moves her fridge and fan cards to a separate pile, keeping her torch card.
setup.caption: 2. Power cut! Every plug card goes out. Cell cards stay.

flow.do: Cut out the cards. Read the rules together. Show one plug card and one cell card.
flow.say: Each card is a thing in a home. Before you turn it over, say plug or cell. Then check the back.
flow.kid: Take a card. Say plug or cell. Then turn it over.
flow.parent: Print the appliance cards two-sided, so the answer is on the back.

flow.do: Play. When a Power Cut card comes up, ask everyone why their plug cards stopped.
flow.say: Power cut! Which of your cards stop working? Why do they stop while the others keep going?
flow.kid: Power cut! Which cards stop? Why?

ask.q: Why does the phone keep working in a power cut?

flow.parent: The phone, laptop, emergency lamp and power bank have batteries that are charged from the wall. They keep working until their battery runs down.

flow.do: Count the working cards. Ask which kind of card was safest to keep.
flow.say: Count your cards. Which kind of card was safest to keep in this game? Why?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Which kind lasted best?

ask.q: Which cards lasted through every power cut?
good: The ones that carry their own electricity.

games.title: Act the Appliance: light, sound, heat, cold or movement?
games.context: This is an acting game. One player acts out an appliance without words. The others guess the appliance, then say what job electricity does in it.
rules: Mix the cards and put them face down.
The actor takes the top card, reads it secretly, and acts it out without words.
The others guess the appliance. Then they say its job: light, sound, heat, cold or movement.
Turn the card over to check the job. One point for the right appliance and one point for the right job.
Take turns being the actor. The first player to 6 points wins.

setup.art: A girl spinning on the spot with her arms out like fan blades, while her father and brother guess.
setup.caption: 1. Act out the appliance on your card.

setup.art: A card turned over to show 'Movement' on the back, beside a small score sheet with tally marks.
setup.caption: 2. Guess the appliance and its job. Check the back.

flow.do: Cut out the cards. Act out the first one yourself, to show how.
flow.say: Watch me. I'm an appliance. What am I? What job is electricity doing in me?
flow.kid: Watch the actor. What appliance is it? What job does it do?

flow.do: Take turns acting. After each guess, ask what job electricity is doing.
flow.say: You guessed the fridge. What job is electricity doing in a fridge: light, sound, heat, cold or movement?
flow.kid: What job does electricity do in it?

good: The TV makes light and sound.
The hair dryer makes heat and blows air.

flow.parent: A fridge's hum is a sound, but its job is to make cold. Accept a good reason for a second job.

projects.title: Our Electricity Week: read the meter for five days
projects.context: In this project you read your home's electricity meter every evening for five days, with a grown-up. The meter counts how much electricity your home uses, in units.

materials.item: your home's electricity meter, or the last electricity bill if you cannot reach the meter
a notebook page with five rows, one for each day
a pencil

projects.safety: Look at the meter only. Never touch the meter box or its wires.

schedule.what: Read the meter at the same time in the evening and write the number.
Read the meter again. Work out how many units were used since yesterday.
Read the meter. Write what was used a lot today: the iron, the washing machine, the geyser?
Read the meter. Try to use one less appliance today.
Read the meter. Find the day with the most units, and say why.

projects.record: A table with five rows: the day, the meter number, the units used since yesterday, and the big appliances used that day.

setup.art: A mother and daughter standing in a building's meter room, the girl pointing at the numbers on one meter and writing in a notebook.
setup.caption: 1. Read the numbers on your meter each evening.

setup.art: A notebook page with five rows of numbers and small drawings of an iron and a washing machine next to one row.
setup.caption: 2. Write the number. Work out the units used since yesterday.

flow.do: Day 1: find your home's meter together. Read the big number and write it down.
flow.say: This meter counts the electricity our home uses. Let's write down the number. Tomorrow we'll see how much it grew.
flow.kid: Read the big number on the meter. Write it down.
flow.parent: Digital meters may show several numbers in turn. Wait for the one marked kWh, which means units. If you cannot reach your meter, look at the units on your last bill and divide by 30 together for a daily number.

flow.do: Days 2 to 4: read the meter at the same time each evening. Take away yesterday's number. Talk about what was used.
flow.say: Take yesterday's number away from today's number. That is how many units we used. What did we use a lot today?
flow.kid: Read the meter. How many units today? What did we use?
flow.parent: Appliances that heat use the most: the geyser, the iron and the electric kettle. An air conditioner uses a lot too.

flow.do: Day 5: look at all five days. Find the biggest day and talk about why.
flow.say: Which day used the most units? What was different about that day?
flow.kid: Which day used the most? Why?

ask.q: Why did one day use more units?
good: Guests came and the fans were on all day.

challenges.title: Light the Dinner Table in a Power Cut
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In a power cut, a torch makes a narrow beam. Can you spread its light so the whole family can see their plates at dinner?
challenges.problem: In a power cut, a torch lights only one small circle. Find a way to light up a whole dinner table using only things that carry their own electricity.
constraints: Use only a torch or a phone torch, and things from home.
Nothing may be plugged into the wall.
No candles or diyas, because we are testing electric light.
materials: a torch or a phone with a torch
a clear plastic water bottle filled with water
a white paper or a white wall
a thin white cloth or a sheet of butter paper
general: An emergency lamp has a battery that is charged from the wall before the power cut.
Many homes have an inverter, a big battery that is filled from the mains and runs fans and lights in a power cut.
Solar lamps fill their battery from sunlight during the day.
creative: Stand a full water bottle on the phone's torch. The water spreads the light all around, like a lamp.
Shine the torch at a white ceiling, so the light bounces down over the table.
Cover the torch with a thin white cloth, so the beam spreads wider.
challenges.your_turn: Try three ways. In which one can everyone see their plate? Draw your best design.

setup.art: A dark dining table with a single narrow torch beam lighting only one plate.
setup.caption: 1. Shine the torch. How much of the table can you see?

setup.art: A phone lying torch-up on the table with a full water bottle standing on it, glowing and lighting every plate around it.
setup.caption: 2. Try a way to spread the light. Can everyone see their plate now?

flow.do: Switch off the room lights in the evening. Shine one torch at the table. Ask for ideas before showing any.
flow.say: The torch lights only one plate. How could we spread the light over the whole table, without using electricity from the wall?
flow.kid: The torch lights one plate. How can you light them all?

good: Use a mirror or a steel plate.

flow.do: Your child tries three ideas, one at a time. Count how many plates you can see for each.
flow.say: Try your first idea. How many plates can you see now? Now try the next one.
flow.kid: Try an idea. Count the plates you can see.
flow.parent: The water bottle on a phone torch works well. A bottle with a little milk in the water spreads the light even more. Keep the phone dry.

flow.do: Talk about which way worked best and why. Your child draws the best design.
flow.say: Which way lit the most plates? Why do you think it worked?
flow.kid: Which way worked best? Draw it.

check.q: Why does the water bottle lamp still work in a power cut?
options: The phone carries its own charged battery
The bottle stores light from the day
check.why: The light comes from the phone's battery, which was charged earlier from the wall. The water only spreads the light out. It does not make any.

worksheets.title: Plug or cell? Where we use electricity

items.p: Sort these into two groups: things that use a plug, and things that use cells.
items.why: Things with a wire and a plug get mains electricity from the wall. Things with a little door for cells carry their own electricity. A strong answer looks for the wire or the cell door.

items.p: Draw a line from each appliance to the job electricity does in it.
items.why: Appliances change electricity into light, sound, heat, cold or movement. A strong answer can say what each one does for us.
items.art: Five appliances on the left (bulb, doorbell, iron, fridge, fan) and five job pictures on the right (sun, music note, flame, snowflake, spinning arrow).

items.p: There is a power cut. Which of these keeps working?
opts: The wall clock with a cell
items.why: The clock carries its own cell, so it does not need the wall. The fan and the fridge get mains electricity, which stops in a power cut.

items.p: Draw one appliance in your home that makes movement. Draw an arrow to show what moves.
items.a: Any appliance that moves, such as a fan with arrows round the blades or a mixie with an arrow round the blade.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the part that moves, so it is clear that electricity makes movement.

items.p: The switch on the wall makes the electricity.
items.why: False. The switch only lets the electricity through or stops it. The electricity comes along wires from a power station. In a power cut, the switch does nothing.

items.p: Why does a torch work in a power cut when the fan does not? Say your answer out loud, and a grown-up writes it down.
items.a: The torch has its own cells inside. The fan gets electricity from the wall, and the wall has none in a power cut.
items.why: A strong answer says where each one gets its electricity: the torch from its cells, the fan from the wall.

items.p: Mains electricity is made in a power ____.
items.why: A power station is a big building where mains electricity is made. It travels to homes along wires.

items.p: In the Tired Cell Test, 6 old cells were tried in the clock. 4 of them ran the clock. How many did not run the clock?
items.why: 6 take away 4 is 2. So 2 cells did not run the clock, and 4 still held some electricity.
items.context: This question is about the Tired Cell Test, where old cells are tried in a torch and in a wall clock.

items.p: Two sisters, Meghna and Ishita, find a cell that cannot light the torch.

views.says: This cell is dead. Throw it away.
Let's try it in the clock first. It might still work there.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Say why. Then say one thing the other sister has right.
items.a: Ishita is wise to test it in the clock, because a cell too weak for a torch can still run a clock. Meghna is right that it is no use for the torch any more.
items.why: A strong answer uses the Tired Cell Test as evidence, and does not call either sister simply wrong.

items.p: Label the picture: power station, tall towers, street pole, meter, fan.
a: power station: on the far left
tall towers: carrying wires across the country
street pole: in front of the building
items.why: Mains electricity travels from the power station, along wires on tall towers and street poles, through the meter, to the fan.
items.art: A path drawn from left to right with empty label lines: a power station, tall towers with wires, a pole on a street, a meter box in a building and a fan in a flat.

worksheets.title: From the power station to your phone

items.p: Three of these get their electricity from the wall. Which one carries its own?
items.why: A wrist watch has a tiny button cell inside. A geyser, an iron and a water pump use mains electricity from the wall.

items.p: In the Tired Cell Test, a cell cannot light the torch but runs the clock. Why?
opts: The clock needs much less electricity than the torch
The clock makes its own electricity
items.why: A torch needs a lot of electricity every second. A clock needs only a tiny amount. A weak cell still has enough for the clock. We checked the torch with a new cell, so it was not broken.

items.p: Your phone's battery number dropped 3 points while it played a video with the torch on. While it rested, it dropped 0 points. Say what this shows.
items.a: Playing a video and shining the torch use more electricity than resting. So the battery empties faster when the phone does more jobs.
items.why: A strong answer compares the two drops and says which job used more of the battery's store.

items.p: Put the path of mains electricity in order, from where it is made to where it is used.
items.why: Electricity is made in the power station. It travels along wires on tall towers, then street poles, through your building's meter, and to the fan.

items.p: Draw a phone being charged. Show where its electricity comes from, and where it goes.
items.a: A phone with a charger wire going to a wall socket, and an arrow from the socket into the phone.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the electricity going from the wall into the phone's battery, where it is stored for later.

items.p: An AA cell from a torch is strong enough to give you a shock.
items.why: False. An AA cell is very weak, so you cannot feel it through dry skin. Mains electricity from the wall is much stronger and can kill. That is why only grown-ups handle plugs.

items.p: Filling a phone's battery from the wall is called ____.
items.why: We charge a phone by plugging its charger into the wall. The battery stores the electricity until we use it.

items.p: Match each power station to what it uses to make electricity.
items.why: Power stations make electricity from falling water, wind, sunlight or burning coal. Most of India's electricity comes from coal.
items.art: Four small pictures on the left: a dam, windmills, solar panels and a power station with chimneys, and four words on the right.

items.p: Your little cousin wants to play with a button cell from an old watch. What will you tell them, and why?
items.a: No, give it to a grown-up. A button cell is small enough to swallow, and a swallowed one can badly burn a child's insides.
items.why: A strong answer gives the rule and the reason: button cells are a real danger to small children if swallowed.

items.p: Sort these appliances by what they do in a power cut.
items.why: A lift, a Wi-Fi box and a tube light use mains electricity. An emergency lamp and a laptop have batteries that were charged earlier from the wall.

items.p: Three people talk about the light in a room.

views.says: The light comes from the bulb.
The light comes from the power station.
The light comes from the river at the dam.

items.ask: Who is right? Can they all be right? Say why.
items.a: They can all be right. The bulb makes the light, using electricity from a power station. If that power station is at a dam, it uses falling river water. Each person names a different step on the path.
items.why: A strong answer follows the electricity back along its path and sees that each person names one step.

items.p: A torch goes dark. Someone says, 'All its cells are completely empty.' How could you test whether that is right?
items.a: Put the cells in a wall clock. If the clock ticks, the cells still hold a little electricity, but too little for the torch.
items.why: A strong answer suggests a fair test with something that needs less electricity, like in the Tired Cell Test.

items.p: Old cells that ran only the clock are put in a TV remote. What will probably happen?
opts: The remote works for a while
The remote makes the cells new again
items.why: A remote, like a clock, needs very little electricity. So weak cells can often run it for a while. Nothing makes old cells new, except charging a rechargeable one.

items.p: Your heart has no plug and no cell. Draw a child, and show where the energy for her heartbeat comes from.
items.a: A child with a heart drawn inside, and an arrow from food on a plate to the heart.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the body's electric signals run on energy from food, not on a plug or a cell.

items.p: A family has a power cut every evening for an hour. Plan which things they can still use, and say why each one works.
items.a: They can use a torch and a clock, because they have cells. A phone, an emergency lamp or an inverter work if they were charged during the day.
items.why: A strong answer sorts things by where they get their electricity, and remembers that batteries must be charged first.

items.p: Every power station in India burns coal.
items.why: False. Most of India's electricity comes from coal, but power stations also use falling water, wind, sunlight and other fuels.

items.p: A wall clock runs for 12 months on one cell. A torch used every night empties a cell in 1 month. How many cells does the torch use while the clock uses one?
items.why: The torch needs a new cell each month, so in 12 months it uses 12 cells. The torch needs much more electricity than the clock. These are made-up numbers, but real clocks do last many months.

items.p: Draw a cell and label it: the plus end, the minus end and the outside cover.
a: plus end: the end with the small bump
outside cover: the metal or plastic wrapper
items.why: A cell has a plus end with a bump and a flat minus end. It must go into a torch or clock the right way round, matching the signs.
items.art: An AA cell lying on its side with three empty label lines: one to the bumpy end, one to the flat end and one to the wrapper.

items.p: Which one does NOT use electricity at all?
items.why: A grinding stone is turned by a person's arms. Its energy comes from the food that person ate. A mixie, a geyser and a doorbell all use electricity.

items.p: Why do we take used cells to an e-waste box, and not throw them in the dustbin?
items.a: Cells have chemicals and metals inside. In the dustbin they can leak into the soil and water. At e-waste, the metals can be used again.
items.why: A strong answer names the harm (chemicals leaking) and the good (metals used again).

quiz.p: What job does electricity do in a tube light?
quiz.why: A tube light changes electricity into light. If you chose cold or movement, look at what the tube light does when it is on.

quiz.p: What job does electricity do in a geyser?
quiz.why: A geyser heats water for a bath. Its small light only shows that it is on.

quiz.p: Where does mains electricity come from?
quiz.why: Mains electricity is made in a power station. A switch only lets it through. Choosing the switch is a common idea, but in a power cut the switch does nothing.

quiz.p: Which of these can a power station use to make electricity?
quiz.why: A dam's falling water spins machines that make electricity. Moonlight is far too weak, and clouds are not used.

quiz.p: In a power cut, which one stops working?
quiz.why: The fridge uses mains electricity from the wall. The torch and the clock carry their own cells.

quiz.p: A phone works in a power cut. Why?
opts: Its battery was charged from the wall earlier
The power cut does not reach phones
quiz.why: A phone has a rechargeable battery. It stores electricity from the wall and uses it later.

quiz.p: In the Tired Cell Test, an old cell does not light the torch. What should you try next?
opts: Put it in the clock to see if it ticks
Open the cell to look inside
quiz.why: A clock needs very little electricity, so it shows whether the cell still has some. Never open a cell. Used cells go to e-waste, not the dustbin.

quiz.p: Why can a weak cell still run a clock but not a torch?
opts: A clock needs much less electricity
A clock is bigger than a torch
A clock has its own power station
quiz.why: A torch needs a lot of electricity every second. A clock needs only a tiny amount, so a weak cell is still enough.

quiz.p: Which rule keeps you safe with mains electricity?
opts: Never touch a plug or socket with wet hands
Push a pencil into a socket to check it
Pull a plug out by its wire
quiz.why: Water lets mains electricity reach your body and give a shock. Never push anything into a socket. A grown-up pulls a plug out by holding the plug itself.

quiz.p: A little child finds a button cell on the floor. What should you do?
opts: Give it to a grown-up at once
Let the child hold it, because cells are safe
Put it in a toy for the child
quiz.why: A swallowed button cell can badly burn a small child's insides within two hours. Give it to a grown-up at once.

videos.title: How does electricity get into our homes?
videos.why: Shows the path of mains electricity: the power station, tall towers, street wires and the home.
videos.check: Found by search: "How does electricity get into our homes?" by Fun Kids Learn, 2 minutes. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Inside a hydroelectric dam in India
videos.why: Shows falling water spinning machines that make electricity, as at the Idukki dam in Kerala.
videos.check: Find real footage of an Indian hydroelectric station, such as Idukki or Bhakra Nangal. Check that the facts said are correct.

videos.title: Sensitive plant (touch-me-not) leaves folding when touched
videos.why: Shows real footage of a plant sensing a touch and acting within seconds, as the leaves fold up.
videos.check: Found by search: "Sensitive Plant (Mimosa pudica) Leaves Folding up in Response to Touch" by 99Chemicals, 2 minutes. A parent may preview it.

applications: Inverters in many Indian homes store mains electricity in a big battery and run fans and lights during power cuts.
Solar lamps fill their battery from sunlight during the day, and light homes and shops at night where power cuts are common.

Doctors use machines that run on batteries, such as a pacemaker inside the chest that keeps a heart beating steadily. Esther Takeuchi, an American engineer, invented batteries used in devices that are put inside the body to help the heart.
A. Lalitha, from Chennai, became India's first woman electrical engineer in 1943. Engineers like her design the machines and wires that bring mains electricity to homes.

spotted.text: Near Kanyakumari in Tamil Nadu, hundreds of tall windmills turn in the wind and make electricity.
spotted.art: Rows of tall white windmills on flat land with palm trees and hills behind.

spotted.text: At the Idukki dam in Kerala, water falling from the reservoir makes electricity for homes across the state.
spotted.art: A tall curved dam between two green hills, with a lake behind it.

spotted.text: At the Barefoot College in Tilonia, Rajasthan, grandmothers from villages around the world learn to build and fix solar lamps for their own villages.
spotted.art: An older woman in a sari carefully soldering a small solar lamp at a workbench, with other women working beside her.

spotted.text: On a city street in Hyderabad or Pune, thick black wires run from poles into every building.
spotted.art: A busy street with a tangle of black wires running from a pole into the balconies of a building.

spotted.text: On rooftops in many cities and villages, families put up blue solar panels to make their own electricity.
spotted.art: Flat rooftops in a town with blue solar panels tilted towards the sky and a water tank beside them.

open_questions.q: How can we store enough of the day's sunlight to run whole cities at night?
open_questions.why_open: Batteries for this are still very costly and use metals that are hard to dig up. Scientists in India and around the world are trying new kinds, such as batteries made with salt.

open_questions.q: What does a touch-me-not plant feel when her leaves fold?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure the electric signal that runs along her stalk. What the plant feels, and how that compares with our own sense of touch, is still argued about.

open_questions.q: Can we make cells that never leak and can always be used again?
open_questions.why_open: Rechargeable batteries help, but they still wear out after many charges. Engineers are still looking for batteries that last much longer.

ask_kids: Which appliance in our home do you think uses the most electricity?
If the power went off right now, what would still work?
How many things with cells can you see from where you sit?
Where do you think the electricity in our wall was made today?
What job did electricity do for you this morning?

jokes.j: Why did the cell go to school?
jokes.a: To get a little more charge!

jokes.j: What did the torch say in the power cut?
jokes.a: Don't worry, I've got this covered. I brought my own cells!

jokes.j: Why was the fan so popular at the party?
What did the plug say to the socket?
Why did the wall clock keep ticking in the power cut?
jokes.a: It never liked depending on the wall!

jokes.j: Why did the phone need a nap?
What is a fridge's favourite kind of music?
Why did the old cell feel happy in the clock?
jokes.a: At last it had a job that was not too hard!

jokes.j: What did the mixie say after making chutney?

maths.problem: In the Tired Cell Test, 1 cell lit the torch and 5 cells ran the clock. How many more cells ran the clock than lit the torch?
maths.explain: Count on from 1 to 5: 2, 3, 4, 5. That is 4 more. So the clock could use 4 more cells than the torch.
maths.context: This is about the Tired Cell Test, where old cells were tried in a torch and in a wall clock.
maths.why_maths: Taking the smaller number from the bigger one shows how many more cells the clock could still use.

maths.problem: In the Listen to the Electricity activity, a child drew 2 things in the Light box, 1 in Sound, 2 in Heat, 1 in Cold and 4 in Movement. Which job did electricity do most in that home? Make a tally chart.
maths.explain: Make one tally mark for each thing. Movement has 4 marks, more than any other box. So in that home, electricity made movement most often.
maths.context: This is about the Listen to the Electricity activity, where a grown-up switched things off and you sorted them by their job.
maths.why_maths: A tally chart shows at a glance which box has the most things.

maths.problem: In the Phone Battery Race, the number went from 70 to 67 in the video test. In the resting test, it went from 71 to 70. Which test used up more of the battery, and by how much more?
maths.explain: The video test dropped 70 take away 67, which is 3. The resting test dropped 71 take away 70, which is 1. 3 is 2 more than 1. So the video and torch used more of the store.
maths.context: This is about the Phone Battery Race, where a phone rested for 8 minutes and then played a video with its torch on.
maths.why_maths: Working out each drop lets us compare the two jobs fairly.

maths.problem: A torch takes 2 cells. A toy car takes 4 cells. A wall clock takes 1 cell. A family has one of each. How many cells do they need to fill all three?
maths.explain: 2 and 4 make 6. 6 and 1 more make 7. So the family needs 7 cells.
maths.context: This is about the cells in a home, the small stores of electricity that torches, toys and clocks carry.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the cells tells the family how many to buy, so they do not run out in a power cut.

warmup.q: Name one appliance that makes light.
warmup.a: A bulb, a tube light, a torch or a TV.

warmup.q: What does a torch carry its electricity in?
warmup.a: Cells, which many people call batteries.

warmup.q: Does a fridge work in a power cut?
warmup.a: No. It uses mains electricity from the wall.

warmup.q: Can a cell too weak for a torch still run a clock?
warmup.a: Often yes. A clock needs much less electricity.

warmup.q: Should you touch a socket with wet hands?
warmup.a: Never. Water helps mains electricity give a shock.

roots.context: We have listened to the appliances at home and named the job electricity does in each. We have followed the wires back to the power station and tested old cells. Now we look at what the Tired Cell Test showed, and at where else electricity is at work: in our bodies, in plants and in the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Tired Cell Test, the cells that could not light the torch still made the clock tick. They still held some electricity. A torch needs a lot of electricity each second, and a clock needs very little. So a cell runs down little by little, and stops a torch long before a clock.
deep_truth.habit: We sort cells into two kinds, new or dead, as if a cell were full one day and empty the next. The Tired Cell Test shows that a cell runs down slowly, and what it can still do depends on how much the job needs.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Tired Cell Test, many old cells that gave no light in the torch still moved the clock's second hand.

three.who_am_i: You run on electricity too. Tiny electric signals carry messages along your nerves and start every beat of your heart, using energy from your food.
three.what_is_life: Every living being uses tiny electric signals. A touch-me-not plant sends one along her stalk when you touch her, and her leaves fold.
three.what_is_this_world: The electricity for the light in your room began far away: in a river behind a dam, in coal under the ground, in the wind or in sunshine on a solar panel.

roots.thread: A bulb's light, a fan's breeze and a fridge's cold seem very different. In your home, all of them are made from the same electricity, coming along the same wires. That electricity is made from falling water, coal, wind or sunlight. The Sun lifts water into clouds, coal is made from plants that grew in sunlight, and the Sun's heat makes the wind. So most of the electricity in your home began as sunlight.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, The Heart of Understanding (1988)
teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper, and you can see a cloud in it. Without the cloud there is no rain, without rain no tree, and without the tree no paper.
teachings.link: Look deeply at the light in your room, and you can see the river at the dam, the coal from the mines and the sunshine on the solar panels. You can also see the people who keep the wires working.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha taught that everything that is made keeps changing. Nothing that is made stays the same.
teachings.link: A cell is made in a factory, and its chemicals change a little every minute the clock ticks. It does not stop all at once. It changes slowly, even when we cannot see it.

science.text: Energy is never made or lost, only changed. A cell's chemical energy becomes light and heat in a torch, and movement in a clock.
How to store enough of the day's sunlight to run whole cities at night, cheaply, is still being worked out.

other_view.view: Electricity is only tiny particles moving through a wire. A plant's electric signal is an automatic response, like a doorbell ringing when it is pressed. It has nothing to do with feeling.

practice.title: Feel your own electricity
practice.say: Sit still and shut your eyes. Put your hand flat on the left side of your chest. Wait until you feel your heart beating. Every beat starts with a tiny electric signal inside your heart. Your heart has no plug and no cell. Count ten beats quietly. Now think about this morning's breakfast. That food is giving your heart its energy right now.
practice.kid: Sit still. Shut your eyes. Put your hand on your chest. Feel your heart beat. Each beat starts with a tiny electric signal. Count ten beats. Your breakfast is giving your heart its energy.

how_we_found_out.who: Michael Faraday, a scientist in London who began as a bookbinder's apprentice, and Joseph Henry, a scientist in the United States
how_we_found_out.when: 1820 (a wire moves a compass) and 1831 (a moving magnet makes electricity)
how_we_found_out.story: In 1820, Hans Christian Oersted, in Denmark, saw a compass needle swing when electricity flowed in a wire near it. So electricity can act like a magnet. Many scientists then asked the opposite question. Can a magnet make electricity? They put strong magnets beside coils of wire and waited. Nothing flowed. Michael Faraday tried too, on and off, for years. He had left school young and taught himself science while working for a bookbinder in London. In 1831, he found the answer. Electricity flowed in his coil only while a magnet was moving in or out of it. When the magnet stopped, the flow stopped. Joseph Henry found the same thing in the United States at about the same time. The wrong idea was that a magnet sitting still next to a wire could make electricity. The magnet has to move. Today, most power stations use this discovery. Steam, falling water or wind spins huge magnets near coils of wire, and the electricity travels along wires to your home.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People expected a strong magnet sitting still beside a coil of wire to make electricity flow. Faraday showed that electricity flows only while the magnet moves.

playtest: Checked in a city flat: the listening activity needs only a fan, a fridge and the wall switches, pressed by a grown-up. The Tired Cell Test needs old AA cells, a torch and a clock. Most homes have old cells in remotes, toys or a drawer. Many cells that fail an LED torch still run a clock, but results vary: if all cells run both, or none runs the clock, that is still a real result. The phone test drop is small, usually 1 to 5 points. The water-bottle lamp works well on a phone torch. The meter project may need the electricity bill if the meter room is locked.

quiz: A cell is a small store of electricity that you can carry around.
A cell holds chemicals that make electricity flow, so a torch or clock works without a wall wire.
In a power cut the fan stops because its cell has run out.
A fan uses mains electricity, and in a power cut none is coming along the wires.
A cell runs down slowly as it is used, giving less and less.
Its chemicals change as the cell is used, so it gives less electricity over time.
A cell that cannot light a torch has nothing left inside.
Many old cells that cannot light a torch still hold enough to make a clock tick.
Mains electricity travels along wires, on poles or under the ground, from a power station to our homes.
Power stations make mains electricity, and wires carry it to every building and socket.
Small cells are safe toys for little children to play with.
A swallowed button cell can badly burn a small child's insides within two hours.
A rechargeable battery can be filled with electricity again from the wall.
Charging it from the wall refills its store, so it can be used again and again.
The small cells in a torch can kill a person like mains electricity.
Mains electricity can kill, but small torch cells are too weak to give a shock.
Appliances change electricity into light, sound, heat, cold or movement.
Electricity is a kind of energy, and each machine turns it into the job it does.
Only animals with brains use tiny electric signals in their bodies.
Plants send electric signals too, like a touch-me-not folding her leaves after a touch.
odd: The fan, fridge and wall light get mains electricity from the wall, but a torch carries its own cells.
The first three change electricity into heat, but a fan changes it into movement.
The three cells are small stores you can carry, but a power station is a big building that makes mains electricity.
Living bodies use tiny electric signals to do their jobs, but a plastic toy is not alive and sends none.
The first three can be filled again from the wall, but an ordinary cell cannot be recharged.
